title: free, ownership and release discipline
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its C rules.
Trace the example and identify data or control flow.
Recognize common failure and safety cases.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: free releases storage previously obtained from an allocation function. After release, the allocated object no longer exists and every pointer to it becomes invalid. Ownership rules identify which part of a program is responsible for releasing each allocation.
understand.whyItMatters: Clear ownership prevents leaks, double-free errors and use-after-free defects, especially when objects are passed between functions.
understand.analogy: Treat each resource and operation as having a clear contract, valid lifetime and failure path.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace the C standard, compiler or library specifications.

explain.narrative:
free releases storage previously obtained from an allocation function. After release, the allocated object no longer exists and every pointer to it becomes invalid. Ownership rules identify which part of a program is responsible for releasing each allocation.

Check object bounds, lifetimes, arithmetic limits and all relevant return values. Compile with warnings enabled and test both normal and failure paths.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The program owns the allocated object, uses it while valid, releases it once and clears its local pointer to reduce accidental reuse.

practise.guidedTask: Draw the ownership timeline from malloc through free.
practise.independentTask: Design a function that creates an object and document whether the caller or callee owns the returned allocation.
hints: free accepts NULL safely, but it must not be passed an invalid or already-freed pointer.
Every successful allocation should have a clear release path.
Setting one pointer to NULL does not clear other aliases to the same allocation.
